Need to search first.I've written notes on all 31 verses below, but the research was cut short. The search tool hit its usage limit after a few searches, and I couldn't open any page in full. Every note comes from the long extracts the search results returned. Those were large for Enduring Word/Guzik, the multi-commentary pages on Bible Hub and StudyLight (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Henry, Poole, Benson, Keil & Delitzsch and others), the NET Bible notes and a few Precept Austin pages. Some biblehub.com commentary pages run several commentaries together without clear breaks, so I only name a commentator where the extract makes it clear.

**What's missing:** I couldn't read anything from desiringgod.org, ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org, wesley.nnu.edu, the Lutheran sites, the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) or bibleodyssey.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so that part of your request isn't covered. As a result, I can't give named Methodist, Lutheran or Anglican positions. Where traditions do disagree, the evidence comes mostly from Baptist, Puritan/Reformed and other older Protestant commentators, plus Calvary Chapel teachers (Guzik, Chuck Smith) and Churches of Christ (Coffman). Catholic and Orthodox views appear only second-hand, as Church Fathers quoted by Protestant commentators. A second session aimed at those sites would fill the gaps.

---

## Verses 1–9: The words of Lemuel's mother

**v. 1 — Who is Lemuel? (a real disagreement)**
- **Traditional reading:** Lemuel appears in no list of Israel's or Judah's kings. He was probably a non-Israelite king who came to trust Yahweh. His name means "belonging to God." The word "utterance" marks his words as revelation, like Agur's in ch. 30. His mother may have been Jewish and taught him the fear of the LORD, much as Timothy was taught (2 Tim 1:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-31/
- **"Lemuel is Solomon":** Matthew Henry says most interpreters think so. He suggests "Lemuel" was a fond pet name his mother used, and he links it to Solomon's other name, Jedidiah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_031.cfm Benson says Jewish and Christian writers generally agree on this. The Geneva Bible notes and Poole identify the mother as Bathsheba. Poole adds that she had repented of her adultery and tried to keep her son from similar sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-1.htm Spurgeon also calls Lemuel "probably Solomon." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html
- **"Lemuel is unknown," possibly "king of Massa":** Ellicott sees no good reason to equate Lemuel with Solomon and prefers the reading "Lemuel, king of Massa." The Cambridge Bible links Massa with an Ishmaelite tribe in northern Arabia (Gen 25:14). It notes that this would mean Israel's sacred library included non-Israelite authors. Keil & Delitzsch also read "king of Massa." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-1.htm Clarke finds no evidence that Lemuel is Solomon. He dates the chapter later because of its Aramaic-style words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/proverbs/31.htm Guzik notes the Jewish legend that Bathsheba gave this advice to Solomon and says there is no evidence for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-31/
- **The mother's role:** The Pulpit Commentary notes that a reigning king's mother ranked even above his wife. It lists other wise women in Scripture, such as Deborah and Huldah, so a king taught by his mother is nothing odd. Gill explains why her teaching is called "prophecy": it was a weighty saying, possibly given under inspiration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-1.htm The Bible Hub study notes stress her influence as an example of women teaching the faith. https://biblehub.com/study/proverbs/31-1.htm
- **Older Greek translation:** The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Septuagint reads the verse quite differently ("My words have been spoken by God…"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown (JFB) say the repeated "What?" shows how earnest she is. "Son of my womb" means "my own son." "Son of my vows" means he was dedicated to God, which may be what "Lemuel" means. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm
- NET: "son" is spelled the Aramaic way (*bar*) all three times. The repetition shows how serious the warning is, and the tender titles show how much she has invested in his place in God's plan. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Joseph Parker suggests he may have been given in answer to her prayers, like Samuel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/parker/proverbs/31.htm Clarke calls the verse very compressed. He thinks Coverdale's paraphrase captures it well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/proverbs/31.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: an excessive sexual interest in women drains a man's strength. Romance and sex have a proper place but must not become a reason for living. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm
- NET: "strength" means physical vigour, and spending it refers to sexual involvement. A king could easily spend his energy that way, but it would be unwise. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:3-5
- Ray Pritchard: a would-be king must discipline himself. Promiscuity leads to moral and spiritual ruin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-ray_pritchard
- GotQuestions links the warning to the later poem: verses 10–31 suit the kind of woman Lemuel should look for. https://www.gotquestions.org/Proverbs-31-virtuous-woman.html

**v. 4 — Kings and wine (a real disagreement)**
- **Moderation reading:** NET says a total ban on alcohol would be unheard of in an ancient court. The likely meaning is drinking to excess, or needing drink. The Hebrew for "crave" is uncertain; one reading gives a ruler who keeps asking "Where is strong drink?" "Strong drink" is probably barley beer. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:3-5 Guzik: the Bible can see wine as a blessing (Ps 104:15), but a dangerous one that leaders may need to give up voluntarily. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm Henry: drink "unkings" a king while it "unmans" him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_031.cfm
- **Abstinence reading:** Coffman (Churches of Christ) says the verse forbids drinking wine at all, not just excess. He applies it to private citizens as much as to kings. Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) compares wine to the "strange fire" of Aaron's sons: a false stimulant in God's service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html

**v. 5**
- NET: "forget what is decreed" means forgetting the law. "Changing" justice may mean reversing decisions or stripping rights. The "oppressed" are literally "children of poverty." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:3-5
- Parker: she bases a personal habit on a great moral reason, that law and justice not be twisted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/parker/proverbs/31.htm Guzik (quoting another writer): justice is her only political concern, not treasury, monuments or armies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm

**v. 6 — "Give strong drink to one who is perishing" (a real disagreement)**
- **Medicine and mercy:** The Pulpit Commentary says wine has a legitimate place as a restorative or medicine, citing 1 Tim 5:23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-6.htm Ellicott: Jerusalem women later gave a drugged drink to condemned criminals because of this verse. Jesus refused it (Matt 27:34) to keep His mind clear. Barnes mentions the Jewish custom of giving wine to mourners. JFB: such drink restores weak bodies and low spirits. Poole: a poor man's excess hurts only himself, but a king's hurts the public. Gill: kings should give their wine to the starving rather than drink it themselves. Keil & Delitzsch: "perishing" means someone heading toward ruin or death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-6.htm
- Matthew Henry: the wealthy should give wine to the sick and the sorrowful, since that is its purpose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html A Bible Hub article compares it to pain relief in hospice care, not permission for recreational drinking. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Proverbs_31_6_on_drink.htm
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** He takes the verse literally first: wine given medicinally to the dying. Then he warns that turning to the bottle for comfort only sinks a person deeper. Finally he preaches it as the "gospel cordial" that only the Holy Spirit can lead a sinner to drink. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html
- **Abstinence (Coffman):** He reads verses 4–6 together as restricting wine to those "ready to perish," not to anyone else. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html
- **Church Fathers (cited second-hand by that Bible Hub article):** Augustine read the verse allegorically, as comfort for sinners perishing without God. Chrysostom used it to urge sobriety on bishops. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Proverbs_31_6_on_drink.htm
- NET: "bitter in soul" means people in deep physical and emotional pain. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=31&verse=6

**v. 7**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the ruined man forgets his poverty, but a drinking king forgets his duty to the needy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-6.htm
- Henry: if they drink soberly, their drooping spirits revive and they can bear their burdens better. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-6.html

**v. 8**
- NET: "open your mouth" means act as their advocate. The "voiceless" can physically speak but cannot defend themselves in court because they are poor or uneducated. The "dispossessed" are literally "sons of passing away," meaning the defenceless. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:8,9
- Henry: this includes those too weak or afraid to speak, or those shouted down in court. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/31.htm Parker: his mother gives the king the job of a lawyer for the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/parker/proverbs/31.htm
- An Enduring Word blog post applies these verses to today's arguments about refugees. It asks whether advocates really listen to the people they speak for. https://post.enduringword.com/concerned-for-the-oppressed-and-needy/

**v. 9**
- NET: "judge righteously" means more than "fairly": the verdict must match the law. "Defend the cause" means advocacy. Championing the poor was, and still is, the ruler's duty (citing Ps 72:4 and Isa 9:6–7). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:8,9

---

## Verses 10–31: The woman of strength, an A-to-Z poem

**Structure:** The poem is an acrostic. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph in v. 10 to tav in v. 31. Guzik, citing Ross, calls it "the ABC's of wisdom," arranged to help memory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm NET marks each letter and notes echoes of Psalm 111. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31 A Precept Austin devotional sees the poem moving outward in rings: marriage (vv. 11–12), home (13–19), community (20–26), back to the home (27–29), then a closing tribute (30–31). https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_illustrations_3

**v. 10 — Who is this woman? (traditions differ)**
- **Traditional reading:** The phrase literally means "a woman of strength." Henry says she is strong through wisdom, grace and the fear of God; the same Hebrew word describes capable judges in Ex 18:21. Her rarity is a warning to look past beauty, money or family when choosing a wife. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/31.htm Benson: the word fits strength of body or of mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-10.htm Clarke: "full of mental energy," worth more than any jewels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-10.html
- **Who the poem is for (Guzik):** It shows men what kind of wife to pray for. It gives women a goal for character shaped by fearing God. It reminds men to grow in wisdom so they are worthy of such a woman. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm
- **Allegorical reading (Gill, a Baptist):** He reads her as the Church, Christ's bride. He rejects reading her as Wisdom (Christ) only because she has a husband in v. 11. He lists other readings: the soul (Gersonides) and Scripture (Nicholas of Lyra). He traces the Church reading to early Christian writers such as Ambrose. Henry's Concise Commentary also asks whether the poem may apply to the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-10.htm Ellicott records that she has been taken as the Law, the Church or the Holy Spirit. The Pulpit Commentary says "spiritual expositors" see a prophetic picture of the Church, but takes her as an ideal woman. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/31-10.htm
- **Rejecting allegory:** Gaebelein says there is no need to read the poem as the Church. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gaebelein/proverbs/31.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** Reading her as a model for godly women is partly valid but not the whole picture. She is a wealthy estate manager, and the poem says nothing about her inner life or religious practice. NET concludes she symbolises wisdom. The poem is a "hymn to Lady Wisdom" written like an ode to a war hero. It pushes back against cultures that saw women as decoration, and it sets a pattern for men too. The phrase "woman of valor" is also used of Ruth (Ruth 3:11). https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=31&verse=10&tab=commentaries&theme=wiki
- **Catholic tradition (second-hand):** Jerome's Latin reading suggests you could search the ends of the earth for her equal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-10.htm

**v. 11**
- NET: "the heart of her husband trusts" stresses that he trusts her completely. The word for "gain" normally means plunder from war: her skill brings returns as rich as war spoils. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Henry: he trusts her faithfulness and her judgement, sure she will cause him neither loss nor shame. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/31.htm

**v. 12**
- NET: "good and not harm" contrasts the path of wisdom with the path of folly. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- **Catholic tradition (Augustine, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary):** It cites his account of his mother Monica, who won over her unfaithful husband through her virtues. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html

**v. 13**
- NET: "selects" means she seeks out materials. She works "in the delight of her hands," meaning she enjoys the work. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=31&verse=13&tab=commentaries
- Pulpit Commentary: she is rich and has servants, yet works gladly because she sees work as everyone's duty and idleness as wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html

**v. 14**
- NET: like a ship, she goes as far as needed to supply her family. The image shows vision and hard work. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Guzik (quoting another writer): the ship image suggests a constant flow of plenty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: servants were common in Bible times. She cares wisely for them, showing compassion beyond her own family. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm

**v. 16**
- NET: "appraises" means careful planning. Proverbs often uses the word for plotting evil, but here it describes a wise investment. "From her earnings" is literally "from the fruit of her hands." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Pulpit Commentary: this woman is a manufacturer, a merchant and a landowner. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html

**v. 17**
- NET: literally "she girds her loins," tucking up her robes so she is ready to work. She starts with vigour, and possibly "rolls up her sleeves." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- JFB: she adds watchfulness in bargaining to her energy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm

**v. 18**
- NET: "sees" is literally "tastes": she knows from experience that her business is good. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- JFB: the lamp may also mean her prosperity does not fade (compare Prov 24:20). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm

**v. 19**
- NET: the two Hebrew words for "hand" contrast strength with fine skill. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Pulpit Commentary: early translators did not recognise the spinning word. The Greek and Latin versions read "useful works" or "strong things." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html
- JFB: she looks down on no honest work, however humble. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm

**v. 20**
- NET: the parallel lines stress her care for the needy, reusing the "hands" words from v. 19. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- JFB: her hard work is what lets her be generous. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm A Precept Austin devotional calls her an example of kindness for all believers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_illustrations_3

**v. 21**
- NET: "snow" stands for cold weather. She does not worry because the household is ready. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31

**v. 22**
- NET: the word for "coverings" is uncertain; Keil & Delitzsch suggest cushions. Fine linen and purple were costly and marked wealth and rank. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:10-27

**v. 23**
- NET: "known" means he is a prominent, respected man. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- One commentary on the Bible Hub verse-10 page says her husband, not she, sits among the elders, and that "her kingdom is the home." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-10.htm

**v. 24**
- NET: "merchants" is literally "Canaanites," meaning Phoenician traders. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31:10-27
- **Women's work and pay:** The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes use this poem to argue that women have a right to work and to keep their wages. It calls idleness more degrading than work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html Compare the "kingdom is the home" comment under v. 23.

**v. 25**
- NET: the clothing image means her virtues show who she is, as clothes do. "She can laugh" means she is confident about the future because she has planned well. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Henry: she finds comfort in her own virtue and shows it to the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-10.html

**v. 26**
- NET: the Hebrew *torat-khesed* ("teaching of kindness" or "faithful instruction") can be read in several ways. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=pro+31%3A10-30
- One commentary on the Bible Hub verse-10 page: heavenly Wisdom, pictured in Proverbs' early chapters, lives in ordinary kitchens and shops, and her words are gentle even in prosperity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/31-10.htm A Bible Hub sermon calls a woman's tongue a sharp tool that must be dedicated to God. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/31-10.htm

**v. 27**
- NET: "bread of idleness" is food she has not worked for. Though wealthy, she lives on her own effort. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=31
- Pulpit Commentary: the Greek version's wording here is obscure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html

**v. 28**
- NET: "rising up" signals something important is about to happen. The grammar draws attention to the husband: a prominent man praises his wife. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31%3A28%2C29
- Precept Austin devotional: such honour comes from a mother's character and from a father who teaches the children to respect her. Praising your wife in public is wise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_illustrations_3

**v. 29**
- NET: "done noble things" uses the same word as v. 10 ("valiant"). "Daughters" can mean "women." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+31%3A28%2C29
- Pulpit Commentary: the Latin and Greek versions narrow the praise to "gathering riches." The Greek's other reading, "done mighty things," is closer to the sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html
- Henry: good women are not as rare as v. 10 suggests, but she excels them all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/31.htm

**v. 30**
- NET: charm can mislead about a person's character, and beauty is a passing vapour. They are not worthless; something is far more valuable. Fearing the LORD returns to the book's theme verse (1:7). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=pro+31%3A10-30
- Pulpit Commentary: the book ends where it began, with the fear of the Lord, as Ecclesiastes 12:13 does. Beauty fades, but goodness lasts and grows richer with age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html
- Guzik: her fear of the Lord shows a real relationship with God. She is a Mary as well as a Martha. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm Henry: piety is the "one thing needful," preferred far above beauty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/31-10.html

**v. 31**
- NET: "give her her due" can mean give her credit or give her a reward. "Gates" means the public places of business and law. Compare Ruth 3:11. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=31&verse=31
- Pulpit Commentary: let her enjoy what her work has earned (Ps 128:2); her deeds speak for themselves. The Greek reads "fruit of her lips" and "let her husband be praised." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html
- **Catholic tradition (Gregory the Great, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary):** he reads "the gates" spiritually as the day of judgement, the gateway to the heavenly kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-31.html
- Henry: if people stay silent, her works will praise her. Truly virtuous women do not seek compliments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/31.htm Guzik quotes Poole making the same point. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-31.cfm JFB: what she produces is her best tribute. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Pro/Pro_031.cfm
